[[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]]: $\Sigma_{jk}

$\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast=n^{-1}\sum_i(X_{n,i}-\bar X_n)
(X_{n,i}-\bar X_n)^{\mathsf T}$.
consumer_exact_proof_use_excerpts: 1.1 Since $t^2\le1+t^4$ for $t\ge0$, the fourth-moment assumption gives $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Then $\|X\|_2\le1+\|X\|_2^2$ gives $\mathbb E\|X\|_2<\infty$, so the coordinatewise mean $\mu$ is finite. Put $Y_{n,i}=X_{n,i}-\mu$ and $M_n=n^{-1}\sum_iY_{n,i}Y_{n,i}^{\mathsf T}$. Then $\mathbb E\|Y_{n,1}\|_2^4<\infty$, since $(a+b)^4\le8(a^4+b^4)$ for $a,b\ge0$. For each $j,k$, the variables $W_{n,i}^{jk}:=Y_{n,i,j}Y_{n,i,k}-\Sigma_{jk}$ are centered and square-integrable because $(Y_{n,i,j}Y_{n,i,k})^2\le\|Y_{n,i}\|_2^4$. The map $y\mapsto y_jy_k-\Sigma_{jk}$ is Borel, so [F1] and [F2] make $(W_{n,i}^{jk})_{i=1}^n$ independent. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_iY_{n,i}$. By [F1] and [F2], the coordinate variables $Y_{n,i,j}$ are independent across $i$. Thus [F4] makes their cross-covariances zero, and [F4] and [F5] give $\mathbb E\|\bar Y_n\|_2^2=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/n$. Also $\|\bar Y_n\bar Y_n^{\mathsf T}\|_F=\|\bar Y_n\|_2^2$ by expanding both squares. For every $C>0$, [F6] therefore gives $\mathbb P(\sqrt n\|\bar Y_n\bar Y_n^{\mathsf T}\|_F>C) \le\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/(C\sqrt n)\to0$. Thus this centered-mean term converges to zero in probability. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For fixed $j,k$, [F4] gives $\mathbb E[(M_{n,jk}-\Sigma_{jk})^2] =n^{-2}\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(W_{n,i}^{jk}) =n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(W_{n,1}^{jk})$. Since $\mathbb E[Y_{n,1,j}Y_{n,1,k}]=\Sigma_{jk}$, $\operatorname{Var}(W_{n,1}^{jk}) =\mathbb E[Y_{n,1,j}^2Y_{n,1,k}^2]-\Sigma_{jk}^2 \le\mathbb E[Y_{n,1,j}^2Y_{n,1,k}^2]$. Summing over $j,k$ and using $\sum_{j,k}Y_{n,1,j}^2Y_{n,1,k}^2=\|Y_{n,1}\|_2^4$ yields $\mathbb E\|M_n-\Sigma\|_F^2\le n^{-1}\mathbb E\|Y_{n,1}\|_2^4$. Consequently [F6] gives, for every $C>0$, $\mathbb P(\sqrt n\|M_n-\Sigma\|_F>C) \le\mathbb E\|Y_{n,1}\|_2^4/C^2$, so $\sqrt n\|M_n-\Sigma\|_F=O_P(1)$ by [F7]. [F3, F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Expanding the centered sum in [F3] gives $\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast=M_n-\bar Y_n\bar Y_n^{\mathsf T}$. For any $\eta>0$, choose $C_1$ so the limsup tail of $\sqrt n\|M_n-\Sigma\|_F$ above $C_1$ is at most $\eta/2$ by step 2.2. For all sufficiently large $n$, the probability that $\sqrt n\|\bar Y_n\bar Y_n^{\mathsf T}\|_F>1$ is at most $\eta/2$ by step 2.1. The triangle inequality then bounds the limsup probability that $\sqrt n\|\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast-\Sigma\|_F>C_1+1$ by $\eta$. This is $\sqrt n\|\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast-\Sigma\|_F=O_P(1)$ by [F7], which is the claimed root-n rate. [F3, F7, step 2.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

For each $\theta$, list the real eigenvalues of $\Sigma_\theta$ in
nonincreasing order and counting multiplicity. The **covariance-PCA
decomposition** is the list of eigenspaces of $\Sigma_\theta$, ordered by
their distinct eigenvalues from largest to smallest. Equivalently, for each
distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$, its component subspace is
$\ker(\Sigma_\theta-\lambda I)$. The top eigenspace is the leading principal
subspace; when its eigenvalue is simple it is a line, and either unit
representative has the same sign-free direction.
The well-definedness result
[[lem-finite-second-moment-covariance-matrix-is-well-defined]] ensures these
covariance matrices are finite, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The
real spectral theorem
[[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] ensures their
eigenspaces span $\mathbb R^p$.

Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

uses.supplier_contract_excerpt:
For each integer $n\ge 1$ the $n$-th **harmonic number** is the finite sum
$$H_n:=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{j},$$
taken over the finite index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ in the rational numbers. For the
empty index set one sets $H_0:=0$, the empty-sum convention. Thus
$H_1=1$, $H_2=3/2$, $H_3=11/6$ and so on, and each $H_n$ is a rational number
determined by the displayed finite recursion on the upper index. These are the
only harmonic values used in the set-cover analysis of this page.

uses.supplier_contract_excerpt:
Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.
